name: Rupturewort (Herniaria hirsuta)
short: Related species H. glabra in rodents: deaths at high single doses (mice); liver and kidney damage at the top 90-day dose (rats). A small trial of a combination in children reported no adverse effects.
text: No safety studies of Herniaria hirsuta on its own were found. The main toxicity data come from rodents given an aqueous extract of a related species, Herniaria glabra, by mouth: in mice, single doses caused dose-dependent adverse effects on general behaviour and deaths (calculated LD50 8.50 g/kg), and in rats dosed daily for 90 days the extract reduced normal weight gain and, at the highest dose, raised the liver enzymes ALT and AST and serum creatinine, with liver cell necrosis and kidney tubular atrophy and inflammation on tissue examination; the extract also lowered blood sugar in rats with normal blood sugar. Those authors concluded that the extract does not appear to have significant toxicity except at high doses. In a randomised trial without placebo that enrolled 34 patients aged 6 to 18 years after stone lithotripsy (two were excluded), a three-component herbal product containing Herniaria hirsuta and Peumus boldus (boldo) was compared with no herbal treatment and no adverse effects were reported; because the product is a combination, this cannot be attributed to Herniaria alone. No interaction data were found in the cited sources.
